source_refs.note: Topic 15.6 (PDF 53-54); Figs 15.11 and 15.13 are redrawn and Fig 15.12 (photograph) is described. The note that the shift occurs at a higher-index surface is added. The check question is Short Answer 15.3, answered; answer needs review.

blocks.text: Bright bands of colour are often seen when light reflects from a thin layer of oil floating on water or from a soap bubble. These are the result of interference. Light waves are reflected from the front and back surfaces of such thin films, and constructive interference between the two reflected waves (which have different path lengths) occurs at different places for different wavelengths. In Fig 15.11, light falling on a thin film of thickness t is partly reflected at the upper surface (path abc); light transmitted through the upper surface is partly reflected at the lower surface (path abdef). The two reflected waves meet at the eye, where, depending on their phase relationship, they may interfere constructively or destructively. Different colours have different wavelengths, so the interference may be constructive for some colours and destructive for others.

blocks.alt: A thin film of index n and thickness t lies on a surface, with air above. A ray a reaches the film at b. Part is reflected along bc to an eye; part enters the film, is reflected at d on the lower surface, comes back up to e and leaves along ef towards the eye.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.11: Thin film (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.11).

blocks.text: That is why we see coloured patterns in thin films, such as the thin soap films that make up bubble walls and thin films of oil on water. The complex shapes of the coloured patterns come from variations in the thickness of the film.

Consider monochromatic light reflected from two nearly parallel surfaces at nearly normal incidence. Fig 15.13 shows two glass plates separated by a thin wedge of air. The path difference between the waves reflected from the two surfaces next to the air wedge is twice the thickness t of the wedge at each point. Where 2t is a whole number of wavelengths we expect constructive interference and a bright area; where it is a half-integer number of wavelengths, destructive interference and a dark area. Where the plates touch there is practically no path difference, so we would expect a bright area.

blocks.alt: Two glass plates touch at the left end; a spacer of height h at distance l holds the upper plate up, enclosing a thin wedge of air. At distance x from the contact the air film has thickness t. A ray falls there and two reflected rays, from the top and bottom of the air film, go up to an eye. Labels: Air, Glass.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.13: Thin film (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.13).

blocks.text: When the experiment is done, bright and dark fringes appear but they are interchanged: along the line where the plates touch there is a dark fringe, not a bright one. This shows that one of the reflected waves undergoes a half-cycle phase shift on reflection, so the two waves reflected at the line of contact are half a cycle out of phase even though their paths are equal. This phase shift can be predicted from Maxwell's equations and the electromagnetic nature of light.
